(`<n>` is the line number of the `pixi run` line in your script.) Ceres
gave the same states, exit codes, and messages. Read them one at a
time:

- **`oom`**: state `OUT_OF_MEMORY`, exit code `0:125`. The log has
  bash's `Killed` line and SLURM's `oom_kill event` line. There is no
  Python `MemoryError`: the kernel stopped the program from outside,
  the `Killed` that @tbl-common-errors said was "often, not always, out
  of memory". `MaxRSS` shows `1G`, **above** the 500 MB request (Ceres
  showed `1045816K`): the kernel kills a moment after the limit is
  passed, and memory is sampled, so read "`MaxRSS` near or above
  `ReqMem`, plus `OUT_OF_MEMORY`" together. This needs a cluster: a
  laptop has no such limit to hit.
- **`timeout`**: the job's own line says `TIMEOUT`, but its `batch`
  line says only `CANCELLED 0:15` (signal 15, the polite "stop" of
  @tbl-signals). Here the reason is on the job's line. The log's last
  line, from SLURM, says `DUE TO TIME LIMIT`.
- **`typo`**: `FAILED`, `127:0` on both lines, and bash's `No such
  file or directory` in the log. Exit status 127 means a command or
  script was not found.

In all three, the script's last line, `echo "end …"`, never ran: the
log shows where each one stopped. `sacct`'s default width cuts
`OUT_OF_MEMORY` to `OUT_OF_ME+` and long job IDs to `17706657.ba+`,
which is why every `sacct` command in this chapter widens those columns
(`JobID%20`, `State%15`).

::: {.callout-note}
## Background: reading `ExitCode` and `COMPLETED`
`ExitCode` is two numbers, `status:signal`. `127:0` is the script's own
exit status (here, "command not found"), with no signal. `0:15` and
`0:125` mean the job was stopped from outside: by signal 15 when the
time ran out, and by the out-of-memory kill. `COMPLETED` only means the
script exited with status 0: it says nothing about whether the result
is right. Check the result.
:::

**Read the records together.** `sacct` gives one line for the job (the
**allocation line**, which holds the request) and one per **step**:
`.batch` is the script itself, `.extern` is SLURM's own bookkeeping,
and a script that runs commands with `srun` gets numbered steps too.
Read those lines **and** the log, because the most useful line varies:
for `TIMEOUT` it was the allocation line, for `OUT_OF_MEMORY` both,
and for `typo` the log.

: Job states. Full list: [`squeue`](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html), "Job state codes". {#tbl-job-states}

| State | Short | What happened | What to do |
|:------|:------|:--------------|:-----------|
| `PENDING` | `PD` | waiting; the reason is in `squeue` | read the reason (@tbl-pending-reasons) |
| `RUNNING` | `R` | running on the node shown | `tail -f` its log |
| `COMPLETED` | `CD` | the script exited 0 | check the result itself |
| `FAILED` | `F` | the script exited non-zero | read the log above SLURM's lines; `127` = not found |
| `OUT_OF_MEMORY` | `OOM` | killed for passing `--mem` | ask for more memory, or give the tool less work |
| `TIMEOUT` | `TO` | killed at `--time` | ask for more time, after checking it was not stuck |
| `CANCELLED` | `CA` | stopped by `scancel`, or a step of a `TIMEOUT` job | check who cancelled it, and why |
| `PREEMPTED` | `PR` | stopped to make room (scavenger) | resubmit, or use a normal partition |
| `NODE_FAIL` | `NF` | the node failed | resubmit; not your fault |

**Then waiting.** A pending job shows its reason in `squeue`'s last
column, `NODELIST(REASON)`. Above, the four jobs submitted together
waited with `(Priority)`; the first job of the chapter showed `(None)`.
Both are normal.

::: {.wide-table}
: Common pending reasons. Spellings as on the sites and SLURM's [reason codes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html). {#tbl-pending-reasons}

| Reason | Meaning | What to do |
|:-------|:--------|:-----------|
| `None` | just submitted, not yet considered (seen on Ceres and Nova) | wait a few seconds |
| `Priority` | jobs with higher priority are ahead (seen on Nova) | wait |
| `Resources` | yours is next, but no node has the room yet | wait; a smaller request may start sooner |
| `Dependency` | waiting for another job (@sec-hpc-slurm-chains) | wait |
| `DependencyNeverSatisfied` | the job it waits for failed, so it can never start | `scancel` it |
| `QOSMaxWallDurationPerJobLimit` | the time asked for is over the QOS limit | fix `--time`, resubmit |
| `PartitionTimeLimit` | the time asked for is over the partition's limit | fix `--time`, resubmit |
| `AssocGrpCpuLimit` (and other `AssocGrp…`) | your group has reached a limit set for the whole group | wait for the group's jobs to finish |
| `ReqNodeNotAvail` | a node it needs is down, drained, or reserved (maintenance is one cause) | wait, or check the site's news |

:::

The two limit reasons appear only on sites set up to accept such jobs;
all three of ours refuse them at submission instead
(@sec-hpc-slurm-layout). For everything SLURM knows about a job, use
`scontrol show job <jobid>`; `squeue --start -u $USER` gives an
estimated start time, which is often empty.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "My job is pending, so something is wrong"
**Reality.** `Priority` and `Resources` are normal waiting; only some
reasons (a limit the request breaks, a dependency that failed) need a
fix. Read the reason column.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Troubleshooting a job
@sec-getting-help-checklist's steps, for jobs: **Where is the log?**
`logs/<name>_<jobid>.out`, or `slurm-<jobid>.out` in the submit folder
if you gave no `--output`. **What does it say?** The last line is
often SLURM's (`DUE TO TIME LIMIT`, `oom_kill event`); the cause is
usually just above it. **Are resources short?** `sacct` shows `State`,
`ExitCode`, `Elapsed`, and `MaxRSS` beside `ReqMem`.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A job's state is `FAILED`, exit code `127:0`. What
is your first guess?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
A command or script was not found: a typo in a name or path, a tool run
without `pixi run` (or without its module), or a relative path that
assumed a different starting folder. The log's last lines name it.
:::
:::

## Measuring a job and sizing the next one {#sec-hpc-slurm-measure}

**Start hands-on.** Ask `sacct` for the fields that compare a request
with its use, for a job that finished. On Ceres, a 2-CPU, 2 GB version
of the read count (captured 2026-11-23):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
sacct -j 22918876 --format=JobID%20,State%15,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,ReqMem,MaxRSS
seff 22918876
```

```{.console}
               JobID           State    Elapsed  AllocCPUS   TotalCPU     ReqMem     MaxRSS
-------------------- --------------- ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------- ----------
            22918876       COMPLETED   00:00:02          2  00:00.246         2G
      22918876.batch       COMPLETED   00:00:02          2  00:00.246               106944K
     22918876.extern       COMPLETED   00:00:02          2   00:00:00
…
Cores per node: 2
CPU Utilized: 00:00:00
CPU Efficiency: 0.00% of 00:00:04 core-walltime
Job Wall-clock time: 00:00:02
Memory Utilized: 104.44 MB
Memory Efficiency: 5.10% of 2.00 GB (2.00 GB/node)
```

Compare cells across lines:

- The **allocation line** holds the request: `ReqMem 2G` (older SLURM
  versions add `n` or `c`, per node or per CPU), `AllocCPUS 2`.
- The **step lines** hold the use: `MaxRSS 106944K` on `.batch`, about
  104 MB. `MaxRSS` is the peak memory of the largest single task in
  that step, sampled every so often: not a total for the step or the
  job (with one task per job, as in this book, it is that task's
  peak). A blank or zero means that line was not measured, or the site
  does not collect it.
- `seff` puts the two side by side: 104 MB used of 2 GB, 5.10%. It
  exists on Ceres, Atlas, and Nova; if your site lacks it, `sacct` has
  everything it uses.

**CPU efficiency by hand.** `seff`'s number is `TotalCPU / (Elapsed ×
AllocCPUS)`: CPU time used, divided by CPU time held. For the two jobs
of @tbl-cpu-efficiency: 7 min 58.9 s is 478.9 s, and 478.9 / (126 × 4)
= 95.0%; the second job's 120.0 / (125 × 4) = 24.0%. Both match `seff`.
For the two-second count above, the CPU time rounds to nothing, so 0%
says only that the job was too short to measure.

: Measuring a finished job. {#tbl-measure-cmds}

| Question | Command | Field | Read from |
|:---------|:--------|:------|:----------|
| How long did it take? | `sacct -j <id> --format=…` | `Elapsed` | the allocation line |
| How much memory did it use? | same | `MaxRSS` (against `ReqMem`) | the step line (`.batch`, or `srun` steps) |
| Were the CPUs used? | same, or `seff <id>` | `TotalCPU`, `AllocCPUS` | either; `seff` divides for you |
| How much disk? | `du -sh` | size | outputs, and the job's own temporary folder |
| How long did it wait? | `sacct -j <id> --format=JobID%20,Submit,Start` | `Start` − `Submit` | the allocation line |

**Then estimate.** Test on a small input, measure, and scale with
care. A small run is not a fair sample (@sec-orientation-data-sizes):
memory often depends on the reference (an aligner's index is the same
size for one sample or a hundred), time on the number of reads. For the
next run of a **comparable job that succeeded**, start from:

- memory: the measured peak plus about 25%;
- time: the measured time, scaled to the new input size, plus a margin.

That is a starting estimate, not a guarantee: sampling can miss a short
peak, and a job killed for memory tells you only that it needed more
than it was given, not how much. For disk, `du -sh` the outputs and the
job's temporary folder. On the GNU/Linux nodes of a cluster,
`/usr/bin/time -v <command>` reports one command's peak memory
("Maximum resident set size") and time directly; macOS's
`/usr/bin/time` has no `-v`.

**The habit.** Record each job's request, what it used, its job ID,
and how long it waited in `NOTEBOOK.md` (@sec-organizing-projects-records).
After a few runs of the same step, you will know its size without
guessing.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A job on the same input as next time shows `MaxRSS`
1.2 GB against `ReqMem` 32 GB, and `Elapsed` 0:04:10 of a 2-day
request. What do you request next time?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
About 1.5–2 GB of memory (the peak plus a margin) and well under an
hour, say 20–30 minutes. The smaller request can start sooner and
leaves the rest of the node for others.
:::
:::

## Job arrays: one script, many inputs {#sec-hpc-slurm-arrays}

@sec-shell-scripts-loops ran one command per sample with a `for` loop,
one after another. On a cluster, the same work is one **job array**:
one script, submitted once, run as many tasks, each with its own number.
The list of inputs is the project's own manifest from
@sec-organizing-projects-metadata, `data/meta/reads.tsv`: one row per
**run**, with columns `sample`, `run`, `fastq_1`, `fastq_2`. Each task
is keyed by its run accession, which is unique where sample labels need
not be.

### More data for the array

An array of one is no array. Add three more paired-end runs of the same
nf-core test set, so `reads.tsv` has four rows. This changes the
project, so do it the careful way, with @sec-organizing-projects-raw's
routine: open `data/raw/` for writing, download from the book's pinned
source, add the checksums the book recorded, check, and close it again.
Do it in the **laptop** project, then send it to the cluster with
@sec-working-remotely-move-project's `rsync` and check there:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
chmod u+w data/raw data/raw/checksums.md5
for run in SRR6357071 SRR6357072 SRR6357076; do
  for r in 1 2; do
    curl -fL -o "data/raw/${run}_${r}.fastq.gz" "{{< var testdata-url >}}/testdata/GSE110004/${run}_${r}.fastq.gz"
  done
done
```

Add these six lines to the end of `data/raw/checksums.md5` (open it in
VS Code and paste them; they are the values recorded in the book's
`data/README.md`), then check all eight files and close the folder:

```{.console}
sample	run	fastq_1	fastq_2
WT_REP1	SRR6357070	data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz	data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
WT_REP1	SRR6357071	data/raw/SRR6357071_1.fastq.gz	data/raw/SRR6357071_2.fastq.gz
WT_REP2	SRR6357072	data/raw/SRR6357072_1.fastq.gz	data/raw/SRR6357072_2.fastq.gz

```

Two runs carry the label `WT_REP1`: the test set groups them to test
merging, though ENA lists them as separate biological samples. This is
exactly why the run, not the label, keys each task.

**One script needs updating.** `src/01_count_reads.sh` counts every
file in `data/raw/`, so its table now has eight rows. But the result
check you added in @sec-shell-scripts-read expects exactly a header and
two rows, and it does its job: run the script now and it refuses the
new table, leaving the old one in place.

```{.console}
read_counts: expected a header and 2 rows
```

That number 3 belonged to the two-file project, as Chapter 8 warned.
Make the check work out the expected count from the same list of files
that seqkit reads. In `src/01_count_reads.sh`, replace the `seqkit
stats` line and the two check lines below it with these four
(@sec-shell-scripts-variables has the lists):

```{.bash filename="src/01_count_reads.sh (replaces three lines)"}
  fastqs=(data/raw/*.fastq.gz)                                  # <1>
  seqkit stats --quiet -T "${fastqs[@]}" > results/read_counts.tsv.tmp
  [[ $(wc -l < results/read_counts.tsv.tmp) -eq $(( ${#fastqs[@]} + 1 )) ]] ||  # <2>
    { echo "read_counts: expected a header and ${#fastqs[@]} rows" >&2; exit 1; }
```
1. A list of the FASTQ files, made once and used twice.
2. `${#fastqs[@]}` is the number of files; a good table has one more
   line, the header.

Run it again from the project folder (`pixi run bash
src/01_count_reads.sh`): it exits 0, `results/read_counts.tsv` has nine
lines (a header and eight 50,000-read rows), and the log's `script:`
line shows a new checksum (`8398b37e…` on the book's copy), which is
what that line is for. A damaged file still stops it: a truncated
FASTQ gave `expected a header and 8 rows` and kept the previous table.
Commit the change and note it in `NOTEBOOK.md` with the new data
(@sec-shell-scripts-git). The first job's numbers earlier in this
chapter, two rows, were from before this step.

Then send the project to the cluster with the `rsync` line from
@sec-working-remotely-move-project (only the new and changed files
travel), and run `md5sum -c checksums.md5` in `data/raw/` there: on
Nova all eight said `OK`.

### The array script

**Start hands-on, no cluster needed.** Save this as
`jobs/02_stats_array.sbatch` (SCINet: your account on the `--account`
line; Nova: delete it):

```{.bash filename="jobs/02_stats_array.sbatch"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=02_stats_array
#SBATCH --account=<project>       # SCINet; Nova: delete this line
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=2G
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out   # %A array job ID, %a task number
# One task per run in data/meta/reads.tsv (line 1 is the header).
# Test without SLURM:  SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID=1 bash jobs/02_stats_array.sbatch --dry-run
set -euo pipefail
task=${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID:?run with sbatch --array, or set it to test}  # <1>
threads=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}                                         # <2>
row=$(awk -F '\t' -v n="$task" 'NR == n + 1' data/meta/reads.tsv)         # <3>
[ -n "$row" ] || { echo "no row $task in data/meta/reads.tsv" >&2; exit 1; }  # <4>
run=$(cut -f 2 <<< "$row")                                                # <5>
fq=$(cut -f 3 <<< "$row")
[ -r "$fq" ] || { echo "cannot read $fq" >&2; exit 1; }                   # <6>
echo "task $task: run $run, file $fq, $threads threads, on $(hostname)"
if [ "${1:-}" = "--dry-run" ]; then exit 0; fi                            # <7>
mkdir -p results
pixi run seqkit stats -j "$threads" -T "$fq" > "results/stats_${run}.tsv.tmp"  # <8>
[[ $(wc -l < "results/stats_${run}.tsv.tmp") -eq 2 ]] || { echo "expected one stats row for $run" >&2; exit 1; }  # <9>
mv "results/stats_${run}.tsv.tmp" "results/stats_${run}.tsv"
echo "task $task finished $(date)"
```
1. SLURM sets `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` in each task. Without it, `:?`
   stops the script with a message that says how to test.
2. The CPU request, passed to the tool below; 1 when testing.
3. Task *n* takes line *n* + 1 of the file, because line 1 is the header
   (`awk`'s `NR` counts rows from 1; @sec-text-tools-sed-awk).
4. `awk` prints nothing, and exits 0, for a row past the end; this
   check turns that into an error.
5. `<<<` hands a string to a command's standard input; `cut -f 2` takes
   the second tab-separated field, the run.
6. Stop early if the file in the table cannot be read.
7. `--dry-run` stops after the checks, so you can test the selection
   anywhere.
8. Each task writes **its own** output, named by run, through a `.tmp`
   name. Read 1 only, to keep the example small.
9. The result check from @sec-shell-scripts-read, for one file: a
   header and one row. seqkit can report a damaged file and still exit
   0, leaving a table with only its header; the `.tmp` name alone would
   then publish it. With the check, a truncated FASTQ stopped the task
   with exit 1 and kept the previous good result (tested on the
   laptop; the cluster captures below came from the script before this
   line was added, which prints nothing when the check passes).

Run the selection for every task number before you submit anything,
one more than you have rows:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID=$i bash jobs/02_stats_array.sbatch --dry-run
done
```

On Nova's login node (captured 2026-11-23; the laptop prints the same
with its own host name):

```{.console}
task 1: run SRR6357070, file data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz, 1 threads, on nova-login-1
task 2: run SRR6357071, file data/raw/SRR6357071_1.fastq.gz, 1 threads, on nova-login-1
task 3: run SRR6357072, file data/raw/SRR6357072_1.fastq.gz, 1 threads, on nova-login-1
task 4: run SRR6357076, file data/raw/SRR6357076_1.fastq.gz, 1 threads, on nova-login-1
no row 5 in data/meta/reads.tsv
```

Four tasks, four runs, and task 5 stops, as it should. (A dry run only
reads a small table, so it is fine on a login node.) Now submit four
tasks from the project folder on the cluster:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}

squeue -u $USER
```

```{.console}
task 2 finished Mon Nov 23 03:17:00 PM CST 2026

-------------------- --------------- -------- ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------------
          17720815_1       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2                  nova18-69
    17720815_1.batch       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2     73768K       nova18-69
   17720815_1.extern       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2                  nova18-69
          17720815_2       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2             nova18-wide-10
    17720815_2.batch       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2     72864K  nova18-wide-10
   17720815_2.extern       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2             nova18-wide-10
          17720815_3       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2             nova18-wide-21
    17720815_3.batch       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2     88156K  nova18-wide-21
   17720815_3.extern       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:00          2             nova18-wide-21
          17720815_4       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:01          2             nova18-wide-21
    17720815_4.batch       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:01          2     72420K  nova18-wide-21
   17720815_4.extern       COMPLETED      0:0   00:00:01          2             nova18-wide-21
```

Four logs, four results (each a seqkit table: 50,000 reads), every task
`COMPLETED 0:0`, and the tasks ran on **three different nodes**.

**Then name it** with @fig-job-array. One submission makes N tasks;
each has the same request and its own `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID`. The tasks
run independently whenever resources allow: at once or one after
another, on one node or several, finishing in any order. That is why
each writes its own output file; two tasks writing one file would
garble it.

::: {#fig-job-array}
{{< svg ../figures/job-array.svg >}}

A job array. One `sbatch --array=1-4` makes four tasks; task *n* reads
line *n* + 1 of `reads.tsv` (line 1 is the header) and writes its own
`stats_<run>.tsv` and log. A fifth task would find no row and stop.
Chapter 8's `for` loop, below, does the same work one run after
another, in one process.
:::

**Managing an array:**

- `--array=1-40%5` runs at most 5 tasks at once: be kind to the queue
  with large arrays.
- `scancel 17720815_3` cancels one task; `scancel 17720815` all of them.
- `sacct -j 17720815` lists three lines per task (`_N`, `_N.batch`,
  `_N.extern`), which is why the `JobID` column needs `%20`.
- Logs use `%A` (the array's ID) and `%a` (the task number) in
  `--output`.
- Each site caps the array size (`scontrol show config | grep -i
  MaxArraySize`): 10001 on Ceres and Atlas, **1001** on Nova. The
  largest task number is one less, so Nova allows `--array=1-1000`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: the header row and the task past the end
With the header on line 1, task *n* must read line *n* + 1, and four data
rows mean `--array=1-4`. A task past the last row gets nothing
from `awk`, which exits 0, so `set -e` alone would not stop it: without
the `[ -n "$row" ]` check, task 5 would run seqkit on nothing. Dry-run
every task number first.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** With the `awk` line as written and four data rows,
what do tasks 0, 1, and 5 read?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Task 0 reads line 1, the header (its "file" would be `fastq_1`, which
the readable-file check stops); task 1 reads the first run; task 5
reads nothing, and the empty-row check stops it. So the array is
`--array=1-4`.
:::
:::

## Chains of jobs (overview) {#sec-hpc-slurm-chains}

**Overview.** @sec-shell-scripts-pipeline ran numbered scripts one
after another with `src/run_all.sh` and promised a cluster version.
The simplest one is a single job that runs `run_all.sh`: its order and
its stop-at-the-first-failure behaviour stay exactly as they are. Make
a copy of `jobs/01_count_reads.sbatch` that runs `pixi run bash
src/run_all.sh` instead, and that is it.

Separate jobs earn their keep when steps need different resources (a
big-memory step, a many-CPU step) or can run side by side. SLURM can
start one job only after another succeeds:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
jid=$(sbatch --parsable jobs/01_count_reads.sbatch)
sbatch --dependency="afterok:$jid" jobs/02_gtf_summary.sbatch
squeue -u $USER
```

`--parsable` makes `sbatch` print only the job ID, which `$( )` saves
in `jid`. (`jobs/02_gtf_summary.sbatch` is a copy of the first job
script that runs `src/02_gtf_summary.sh`; making it is exercise 5.)
While the first job waits or runs, `squeue` shows the second as
`(Dependency)`. `afterok` imposes the order you chose; it passes no
data. Here the two steps do not even need each other's output, so
`afterok` only says "not before". If you did @sec-shell-scripts's
exercise 4, `src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh` can be submitted with no
dependency at all, beside `02`, and you can watch both run at once.

**When the first job fails**, `afterok` never starts the second. What
happens to it then depends on the site (captured 2026-11-23, with a
first job that failed):

- **Ceres and Nova** leave it pending for ever, as
  `(DependencyNeverSatisfied)`. Cancel it yourself with `scancel`, or
  submit it with `--kill-on-invalid-dep=yes` so SLURM cancels it.
- **Atlas** cancels it automatically (its configuration has
  `kill_invalid_depend`): the second job went from `PD (Dependency)`
  to `CANCELLED` with no `scancel`.

So after a failed chain, check `squeue`: on some sites the job waits
forever, on others it is gone. This is also where hand-made chains
stop being fun. A workflow manager (@sec-workflow-managers) tracks
which steps are done, reruns only what changed, and submits each step
as a job for you; nf-core pipelines do exactly this on SLURM
(@sec-nf-core).

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** The first job of a chain fails. What happens to the
second?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
It never starts. Depending on the site it stays pending as
`DependencyNeverSatisfied` (Ceres, Nova: `scancel` it) or is cancelled
automatically (Atlas).
:::
:::

## GPU partitions (overview) {#sec-hpc-slurm-gpu}

**Overview.** A GPU is asked for like any other resource, with
`--gres` (generic resources), and usually in a GPU partition:

```{.bash filename="jobs/gpu_test.sbatch (the request)"}
#SBATCH --partition=<gpu partition>
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
```

Inside the job, `nvidia-smi` shows the card you got. Only tools built
for GPUs use one: deep-learning tools, NVIDIA's Parabricks, some
basecallers. An ordinary tool on a GPU node leaves the GPU idle while
someone who needs it waits.

The exact form is site-specific (observed 2026-11-23):

- **Atlas** has four GPU partitions, `gpu-v100`, `gpu-a100`,
  `gpu-a100-mig7`, and `gpu-l40s`, with QOS limits of 2 days (7 for
  `a100`). `sinfo -o "%P %G"` names the cards, for example
  `gpu:nvidia_a100_1g.10gb:56` on the MIG partition (an A100 split into
  slices). Use the name `sinfo` shows, or plain `gpu:1`: the
  OnDemand form's `gpu:a100_1g.10gb:1` was refused with `Requested node
  configuration is not available`.
- **Nova** has no separate GPU partition: GPU nodes sit in the default
  `nova` partition (and `interactive`, `scavenger`), and the card type
  goes in `--gres`, for example `--gres=gpu:a100:1`.
- **Ceres** has no GPUs.

Check a request without submitting it with `sbatch --test-only`, which
says when and where the job would start, or refuses it. GPUs in depth
are @sec-gpu.

## Etiquette and a checklist {#sec-hpc-slurm-etiquette}

**Start with a quick audit**, on the login node: what are you running
here, what do you have queued, and how full is your storage?

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
ps -u "$USER"
squeue -u $USER
my_quotas                                  # SCINet; Nova: cat /work/<group>/group_storage_usage
```

`ps` (@sec-linux-system-processes) should show your shell, perhaps
tmux and an editor, and nothing heavy.

::: {.wide-table}
: Sharing a cluster. {#tbl-etiquette}

| Do | Don't | Why |
|:---|:------|:----|
| edit, `sbatch`, small file moves, `module spider` on login nodes | align, sort big files, install large environments, or loop over samples on login nodes | the login node is shared by everyone logged in |
| measure a test run, then request a margin over it | request whole nodes or days "to be safe" | idle reservations block others and can wait longer |
| one array for many inputs, throttled (`%5`) | thousands of separate tiny jobs | each job costs the scheduler work |
| pass the CPU count to the tool | reserve CPUs the tool never uses | idle CPUs are wasted for everyone |
| delete your own temporary folders and scratch copies | leave data in scratch to be purged | purges lose data you forgot; quotas fill |
| `scancel` jobs and sessions you no longer need | leave a held node or OnDemand session idle | it keeps charging and blocking |
| use GPU partitions only for GPU tools | run CPU-only work on GPU nodes | GPUs are scarce |

:::

`scancel -u $USER` cancels **all** your jobs at once; use it with care.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "I can run my analysis on the login node"
**Reality.** The login node is the front desk: shared by everyone, for
editing, submitting, and small moves. Analyses run as jobs on compute
nodes, interactive for trying things, batch for everything longer than
a few minutes.
:::

## Summary {#sec-hpc-slurm-summary}

- A cluster is many computers behind a queue. The login node is for
  editing and submitting; work runs as **jobs** on compute nodes,
  started by SLURM when resources are free. Inside a job, the
  allocation (`SLURM_*`, `scontrol show job`), not `free`, says what
  you may use.
- A request names a partition, an account, and sometimes a QOS, and
  each layer can set limits. `sinfo` is not always the real limit:
  check `scontrol show partition` and `sacctmgr show qos`.
- Home is small; projects hold your work; scratch is big but purged;
  node-local `$TMPDIR` lasts one job. Count files as well as bytes.
  Stage work in a temporary folder of your own and copy results back.
- Load modules by named version inside job scripts, never in
  `~/.bashrc`; use `pixi run` for what the book environment has, and
  never both for one tool.
- `srun --pty bash -l` and `salloc` are interactive jobs; check
  `hostname` after `salloc`, and give back what you hold. To SSH to a
  compute node: hold it, find it in `squeue`, connect with `ProxyJump`,
  `scancel` it.
- A job script is a bash script with `#SBATCH` lines first. Submit
  from the project folder with `mkdir -p logs` done; the job starts
  there with a copy of your environment and no terminal. Check
  `sacct`, the log, **and** the result: `COMPLETED` only means exit 0.
- Ask for CPUs × memory × time on one node, always setting `--time` and
  `--mem`; pass the CPU count to the tool; check `AllocCPUS`. Smaller,
  accurate requests can start sooner.
- Failures read as `OUT_OF_MEMORY 0:125`, `TIMEOUT` (with `.batch`
  `CANCELLED 0:15`), or `FAILED 127:0` for a missing command; read the
  allocation line, the step lines, and the log together. `Priority` and
  `Resources` are normal waiting.
- Size the next run from the last: peak memory plus about 25%, time
  scaled to the input, recorded in `NOTEBOOK.md`.
- A job array runs one script over many inputs; dry-run every task
  number, guard the row past the end, and give each task its own
  output. `afterok` chains jobs; a failed chain waits forever on some
  sites.

@tbl-slurm-commands collects the chapter's commands.

::: {.wide-table}
: The chapter's commands on one page. {#tbl-slurm-commands}

| Task | Command |
|:-----|:--------|
| Partitions and their limits | `sinfo -s`, `scontrol show partition <name>` |
| Your accounts and QOS | `sacctmgr -n -P show assoc user=$USER format=account,partition,qos,defaultqos`, `sacctmgr show qos` |
| Node sizes | `sinfo -N -o "%N %c %m %G"` |
| Interactive shell | `srun --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=4G --time=00:30:00 --pty bash -l` (SCINet: `-A <project>`) |
| Hold a node | `salloc -N1 -n1 --time=00:20:00 --mem=2G sleep infinity`, then `scancel <jobid>` |
| Submit | `sbatch jobs/script.sbatch`; `sbatch --array=1-4 …`; `jid=$(sbatch --parsable …)` |
| Your jobs | `squeue -u $USER`; `squeue --start -u $USER` |
| Everything about one job | `scontrol show job <jobid>` |
| What a job used | `sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID%20,State%15,ExitCode,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,ReqMem,MaxRSS`; `seff <jobid>` |
| Cancel | `scancel <jobid>`, `scancel <jobid>_3`, `scancel -u $USER` (all) |
| Check a request | `sbatch --test-only …` |
| Modules | `module spider <name>`, `module load <name>/<version>`, `module list`, `module purge` |
| Site settings | `scontrol show config \| grep -i -E 'MaxArraySize\|NamespaceType'` |

:::

## Exercises {#sec-hpc-slurm-exercises}

Exercises 1–4 are core; 5 and 6 are optional. Each has a route without a
cluster. Record what you did and saw in `NOTEBOOK.md`, in the project
for the cluster parts and in `~/bioinf-computing-ch10` for the rest.

::: {.check}
**Exercise 1. Know your cluster.** After @sec-hpc-slurm-layout and
@sec-hpc-slurm-storage.

Fill a five-row card in `NOTEBOOK.md` for your site: the default
partition and its real time limit (and where that limit comes from);
your accounts; the interactive partition, if any; the quota command
and your current use; whether `seff` exists.

**No cluster?** Fill the card for this fictional site from its outputs
and one sentence of its user guide ("Interactive sessions: use the
`short` partition."):

```{.console}
$ sinfo -s
PARTITION AVAIL  TIMELIMIT   NODES(A/I/O/T) NODELIST
main*        up 30-00:00:0       40/10/2/52 n[001-052]
short        up    4:00:00         2/6/0/8 s[01-08]
$ scontrol show partition main | grep -o -E '(DefaultTime|MaxTime|QoS)=[^ ]+'
QoS=main
DefaultTime=01:00:00
MaxTime=30-00:00:00
$ sacctmgr -n show qos format=Name%10,MaxWall | grep main
      main  7-00:00:00
$ sacctmgr -n show assoc user=$USER format=account%20
            lab-smith
$ command -v seff || echo "no seff"
no seff
$ site_quota
Path                      Used (GB)   Quota (GB)   Files     File quota
/home/<user>                    4.1         20      31,207     200,000
/proj/lab-smith              1840.0       5000   2,914,330   5,000,000
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
For the fictional site: default partition `main`, whose real limit is
7 days, from the `main` QOS the partition attaches (`sinfo` says 30);
account `lab-smith`; interactive partition `short` (4 hours; it is the
user guide that says so, not the time limit); quota command
`site_quota`: home 4.1 of 20 GB, the project 1,840 of 5,000 GB, and
this site also counts files (2.9 of 5 million in the project); no
`seff`, so measure with `sacct`. (`df -h` would show the file system's
free space, not your quota.) On a real site, compare with
@tbl-sites-slurm.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 2. Adapt the first job.** After @sec-hpc-slurm-first-job.

Copy `jobs/01_count_reads.sbatch` to `jobs/count_small.sbatch`. Give it
the job name `count_small`, 1 GB of memory, and 5 minutes. Before
submitting, write down the log file's name. Submit it, and confirm with
`sacct`, the log, and `results/read_counts.tsv`. Then give a log a date
in its name. `#SBATCH` lines are not expanded, so do it on the command
line, where your shell fills in the date before `sbatch` runs:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
sbatch --output="logs/%x_%j_$(date +%F).out" jobs/count_small.sbatch
```

**No cluster?** Run the copy with `bash` on the laptop, and write down
what the log would have been called.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`logs/count_small_<jobid>.out`. `sacct` shows `COMPLETED 0:0` with
`ReqMem 1G`; the log has the start line, Chapter 8's lines, and the
finish line; the result file has one 50,000-read row per FASTQ file
(eight after the array's data step). The dated version wrote, on Nova,
`logs/01_count_reads_17720578_2026-11-23.out` for the original script:
`%x` and `%j` are SLURM's, the date was the shell's. With `bash`, there
is no log file at all: everything goes to your terminal.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 3. Diagnose three failures.** After
@sec-hpc-slurm-failures.

Submit `ok.sbatch`, then the three broken scripts. For each, record
`State`, `ExitCode`, and the one log line that explains it. Then fix
one of them, resubmit, and confirm it completes: give `oom` more
memory than it takes (`--mem=3G`), or `timeout` more time than it
sleeps (`--time=00:10:00`). If you choose `typo`, fix the spelling
first and submit it: it fails again, for a different reason. Find that
reason in the log, and fix it too.

**No cluster?** Use the captured `sacct` table and logs in
@sec-hpc-slurm-failures, and answer from these three lines of another
user's jobs as well:

```{.console}
               JobID           State ExitCode    Elapsed     ReqMem     MaxRSS
            31337001   OUT_OF_MEMORY    0:125   00:42:10        16G
      31337001.batch   OUT_OF_MEMORY    0:125   00:42:10                 16.4G
            31337002         TIMEOUT      0:0   12:00:16         64G
      31337002.batch       CANCELLED     0:15   12:00:18                  3.1G
            31337003       COMPLETED      0:0   00:03:05        120G
      31337003.batch       COMPLETED      0:0   00:03:05                  2.2G
```

Which ran out of memory, which hit its time limit, and which asked for
far more memory than it used?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`ok`: `COMPLETED 0:0`, log `ok`. `oom`: `OUT_OF_MEMORY 0:125`, log
`… Killed …` and `Detected 1 oom_kill event`. `timeout`: `TIMEOUT 0:0`
(`.batch` `CANCELLED 0:15`), log `CANCELLED AT … DUE TO TIME LIMIT`.
`typo`: `FAILED 127:0`, log `No such file or directory`. With the
spelling fixed, `typo` fails with `run from the project folder`: the
job starts in the scratch folder, and Chapter 8's guard stops the
script there, as it should. A path to the script finds the script; it
does not change the folder the script runs in, nor start the book
environment that `seqkit` needs. The full fix replaces the `bash` line
with `cd "$project"` and `pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh`. In the
extra table: 31337001 ran out of memory (its peak passed 16 GB);
31337002 hit its 12-hour limit (and used only 3.1 of 64 GB, so the next
request needs more time but far less memory); 31337003 used 2.2 of 120
GB, so about 3 GB would do.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 4. Right-size a request.** After @sec-hpc-slurm-measure and
@sec-hpc-slurm-arrays.

Run `jobs/02_stats_array.sbatch` as an array over the four runs with a
generous request (8 CPUs, 16 GB, 1 hour, given on the command line:
`sbatch --array=1-4 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=16G --time=01:00:00 …`).
Use `sacct` or `seff` to choose a smaller memory and time request, and
resubmit with it. For both runs, record peak memory, elapsed time, and
queue wait (`sacct -j <id> --format=JobID%20,Submit,Start`) in
`NOTEBOOK.md`. Wait times depend on the queue at that moment, so record
them; do not expect a "right" answer. These tasks last a second or
less, too short for CPU efficiency to mean anything (it will likely
read 0%, as for the first job). For the CPU part, use the two
2-minute jobs in @tbl-cpu-efficiency instead: compute each one's
efficiency by hand from `TotalCPU`, `Elapsed`, and `AllocCPUS`, and
say how many CPUs you would ask for to run the second one again.

**No cluster?** Choose the smaller request from the four captured
tasks in @sec-hpc-slurm-arrays (2 CPUs, 2 GB, at most 1 second each),
and do the CPU part as above.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Each task peaked at 72–88 MB and ran a second or less, so about
256–512 MB (the peak plus a margin, rounded up generously for such a
small number) and a few minutes is plenty; keep 1–2 CPUs, since a
second-long task gains nothing from more. The smaller request often
waits less, but not always. CPU part: 478.9 s / (126 s × 4) = 95.0%
and 120.0 s / (125 s × 4) = 24.0%; the second job kept one CPU busy,
so it needs 1 CPU (or its tool told to use 4).
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 5 (optional). Chain two steps.** After
@sec-hpc-slurm-chains.

Make `jobs/02_gtf_summary.sbatch` by copying the first job script and
changing the job name and the `pixi run` line to `src/02_gtf_summary.sh`.
Submit it with `--dependency="afterok:$jid"` after the first job, and
watch `squeue`. Then make the first job fail (submit `typo.sbatch`, or
point the first script at a missing file), chain the second after it,
and record what your site does with the second.

**No cluster?** From @sec-hpc-slurm-chains, write down what you would
expect on Ceres and on Atlas, and the command that cleans up on Ceres.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
With a successful first job, the second shows `(Dependency)`, then
runs. After a failed first job, Ceres and Nova leave the second
pending as `(DependencyNeverSatisfied)`, and `scancel <jobid>` removes
it; Atlas cancels it by itself.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 6 (optional). Use temporary space in the array.** After
@sec-hpc-slurm-storage and @sec-hpc-slurm-arrays.

Copy the array script to `jobs/02_stats_staged.sbatch` and add the
staging pattern from `jobs/ch10_staging.sbatch`: each task makes its
own folder under `$TMPDIR` (with `${SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID}_${task}` in its
name), copies its FASTQ file there, runs seqkit on the copy, copies
`stats_<run>.tsv` back to `results/`, and removes its folder. Confirm
the four results match the unstaged ones (`diff`) and that each log
shows its folder gone. With tiny files the time will not change; the
habit is the point.

**No cluster?** Run it on the laptop with `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID=1 bash
jobs/02_stats_staged.sbatch`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
One possible core, after the checks:

```bash
project=$PWD
work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:?}/stats_${SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID:-local}_${task}_XXXX")
cp "$fq" "$work/"
pixi run seqkit stats -j "$threads" -T "$work/$(basename "$fq")" > "$work/stats.tsv"
[[ $(wc -l < "$work/stats.tsv") -eq 2 ]] || { echo "expected one stats row for $run" >&2; exit 1; }
cp "$work/stats.tsv" "$project/results/stats_${run}.tsv.tmp"
mv "$project/results/stats_${run}.tsv.tmp" "$project/results/stats_${run}.tsv"
rm -rf "$work"
```

The table's first column now shows the temporary path instead of
`data/raw/…`, so `diff` reports that column; compare the other columns
with `cut -f 2- results/stats_SRR6357070.tsv`.
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-hpc-slurm-reading}

- @hpccarpentry2026intro, *Introduction to High-Performance Computing*
  --- a hands-on lesson on the same ground (logging in, the scheduler,
  job scripts, modules, transferring files), with exercises; good for a
  second explanation of anything here.
- @schedmd2026quickstart, the SLURM *Quick Start User Guide* --- the
  official short tour of every command in this chapter, with links to
  each command's manual page; read the `sbatch` and `sacct` pages for
  the options and fields in @tbl-sbatch-options and @tbl-measure-cmds.
- @yoo2003slurm, "SLURM: Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management"
  --- the original paper by SLURM's designers: why a scheduler is built
  around partitions, jobs, and job steps.
- @lmod2026docs, the *Lmod* user guide --- `module spider`, defaults,
  and hidden modules, for when your site's module trees surprise you.
- Your site's own pages: SCINet's [SLURM
  guide](https://scinet.usda.gov/guides/use/slurm) and [Ceres and Atlas
  differences](https://scinet.usda.gov/guides/resources/CeresAtlasDifferences),
  MSU's [Atlas documentation](https://docs.hpc.msstate.edu/), and ISU's
  [SLURM page](https://research.it.iastate.edu/slurm) --- the authority
  for limits, partitions, and storage rules; @sec-cluster-sites collects
  the details.
